title: Force push without deleting your colleague's commit
summary: You rebased a pushed branch, so you must force. Do it the reckless way and destroy a commit; do it with --force-with-lease and watch git refuse to.
concepts: recovering from a bad force push
mental_model: `--force` says 'make the server's branch equal mine, whatever it currently is'. `--force-with-lease` says 'make it equal mine, but only if it still equals what I last saw'. The second is a compare-and-swap; the first is a blind write.
danger: A plain `--force` on a shared branch permanently deletes commits from the server's history. They survive only in the reflog of whoever pushed them.

setup.run: git commit -q -a --amend -m "Add API GET handler with docstring"

steps.title: See the situation you are in
steps.why: You amended a commit that was already pushed, so your branch and the server's have diverged. Meanwhile your colleague pushed a commit on top of the original — which you have not fetched and do not know about.
steps.expect: Your amended commit locally; origin/feature/api still at the old one you pushed.

steps.title: A normal push is rejected, correctly
steps.why: Non-fast-forward. Git is telling you the server has something your branch does not contain — in this case both the original commit and your colleague's work.

steps.title: Try the safe force — and get refused
steps.why: `--force-with-lease` compares the server's current tip with your remote-tracking ref. They differ, because your colleague pushed. Git refuses, and that refusal has just saved their commit.
steps.expect: ! [rejected] ... (stale info). This is the feature working.

verify.label: your cached view of the branch is stale — it has no idea their commit exists

steps.title: Do what the refusal is asking
steps.why: Fetch, look at what arrived, and decide. The lease did not stop you working — it stopped you working blind.
steps.expect: Their POST handler commit appears, sitting on the original version of your commit.

verify.label: you can now see the commit you were about to destroy

steps.title: Rebase their work onto your amended commit
steps.why: Their commit belongs on top of your improved version. `--onto` moves just their commit across, and now your branch contains everything — no force needed to be destructive, only to be a rewrite.
commands: sh -c 'git rebase --onto HEAD $(git rev-parse origin/feature/api~1) origin/feature/api'
steps.expect: Detached HEAD with both commits — yours amended, theirs replayed on top.

steps.title: Move your branch to the combined result
steps.why: The rebase left you detached; pointing feature/api at this commit makes it the branch tip. Now the branch is a strict superset of what the server has, plus your rewrite.

verify.label: your branch now has both your amended commit and their work
verify.hint: rebase their commit onto yours before forcing

steps.title: Now force safely
steps.why: The lease compares against your remote-tracking ref, which you refreshed with the fetch. It matches, so the push goes through — rewriting your commit while preserving theirs.

steps.title: Check the server
steps.why: The bare repository is the source of truth. Both commits are there, and nobody's work was deleted — which is the entire point of the extra six characters in the flag.
steps.expect: Two commits: your amended one, and theirs.

verify.label: the server has both your rewrite and your colleague's commit
verify.hint: fetch, rebase their commit onto yours, then --force-with-lease

verify.label: three commits total — nothing lost, nothing duplicated
verify.hint: a plain --force here would have left only two, deleting their work

verify.label: the file on the server contains your rewrite and their addition
verify.hint: the rebase replayed their commit on top of your amended one

pitfalls: `--force-with-lease` is only meaningful if you have not just fetched. Fetching refreshes the lease, so `git fetch && git push --force-with-lease` is nearly as blind as `--force`. Fetch, LOOK, then push.
`--force-if-includes` (git 2.30+) closes that gap: it also requires that your branch actually contains what you fetched.
Never force-push a branch other people build on without telling them. Their next pull will be a mess regardless of which flag you used.
If someone force-pushes over your commit, it is still in your local reflog. Push it back before your reflog expires.
cheatsheet: force, but only if the server matches what you last saw
…and only if you have integrated it
blind overwrite — avoid on shared branches
